query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In stainless and low‐alloy steels used in chemical‐processing and nuclear-power applications, nanoscale short‐range ordering (SRO) of chromium (and, to a lesser extent, molybdenum) at grain boundaries and interfaces promotes the rapid formation and stability of a protective, self-healing Cr-rich oxide (Cr2O3) layer that suppresses both uniform and localized corrosion in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional Cr‐containing austenitic or low‐alloy steel with a relatively homogeneous (disordered) solid solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal pre‐treatment (annealing) designed to enhance the short‐range ordering of chromium atoms and induce nanoscale compositional clustering prior to exposure to corrosive environments.
generation.conditions: Exposure to aggressive environments representative of chemical‐processing (e.g., saline or acidic solutions at moderate temperatures) and nuclear-power (e.g., high-temperature/high-pressure water with oxidizing conditions) applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Cr-enriched clusters at grain boundaries and near-surface regions that serve as sites for preferential oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced Cr SRO lowers the energy barrier for Cr2O3 formation and leads to a denser, more adherent passive film. This ordered arrangement minimizes defects in the oxide scale, reducing electrolyte penetration and anodic dissolution, while also promoting self-healing upon mechanical or chemical damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels pre-treated to enhance Cr short-range order will show significantly lower corrosion current densities, reduced weight loss, and more stable passivation behavior compared to as-received (more chemically disordered) steels when tested under identical aggressive conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated steels with a nominally disordered distribution of Cr atoms that form less protective and non-uniform passive oxide layers under corrosive exposure.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold under standard aggressive aqueous environments encountered in processing plants and reactor primary circuits; however, its influence may be diminished if other degradation mechanisms (such as irradiation-induced transmutation or high-temperature carburization) predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of improvement attributable solely to enhanced Cr SRO remains uncertain, as other factors (e.g., grain size, inclusion content, and additional alloying elements) also influence corrosion resistance. Further in-depth microstructural and electrochemical studies are needed to isolate and quantify the SRO effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare batches of a Cr-containing steel with identical chemical compositions but differing microstructures. One set is thermally treated to induce enhanced Cr short-range order (via controlled annealing), while a control set is left as-received. Both sets are then exposed to standardized corrosive environments (e.g., simulated PWR primary water and saline acid solutions) under identical temperature, pressure, and flow conditions.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to monitor passive film stability.
Potentiodynamic polarization to measure corrosion current densities and potentials.
Weight loss measurements after fixed exposure times.
Advanced microscopy (e.g., TEM/APT) to verify the extent of Cr ordering and passive film thickness/composition.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated steel (with enhanced Cr short-range order) does not exhibit statistically lower corrosion current densities, reduced weight loss, or demonstrably more uniform and adherent Cr-rich passive films compared to the control set under all tested conditions, then the hypothesis that Cr SRO is a governing cause of improved corrosion resistance will be falsified.

Combined effect of interstitial-substitutional elements on dislocation dynamics in nitrogen-added austenitic stainless steels

Abstract: Combined addition of interstitial-substitutional elements has been acknowledged to contribute to the increase in the strengths of steels. For further improvements in mechanical properties, their atomic-scale interaction mechanisms with dislocations are required to be examined. In this study, both high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and atom-probe tomography were used to correlate interstitial-substitutional elements with dislocation characteristics in austenitic stainless steels. Three types of dislocation core structures are identified and associated with their strain fields as well as N and Cr atoms in the N-added steels. It is revealed that N atoms interact elastically with the dislocations, followed by the segregation of Cr atoms via the chemical interaction between N and Cr atoms. This insight significantly improves the understanding of the multiple alloying mechanism in metallic materials such as interstitial alloys and high-entropy alloys.

Data-driven electron-diffraction approach reveals local short-range ordering in CrCoNi with ordering effects

Abstract: The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys
